name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,152

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Victim of Telamon people heard from across the pond?

indicators.note: something heard reaches the ear rather than the eye, so the spelling is not to be trusted

blocks.note: folks is the everyday American word for people, and a drawled American version comes out with two syllables
no letters: it says the word and the accent are American, the pond being the Atlantic

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the man Telamon killed belongs to a nation on the far side of the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From across the pond' means from America: Americans say folks for people, and the setter imagines it stretched into two syllables. In Greek myth Telamon killed his half-brother during a game of discus or a hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Phocus was the son of Aeacus whose death at the hands of his half-brother Telamon got the killer banished from Aegina.

clue.text: Finnish poet deeply set on leaving wife

indicators.note: whatever is left behind drops out, so a letter goes missing from the word it belonged to

blocks.note: hollow eyes or cheeks are sunken, set deep in the face
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A Finnish poet is firmly determined to walk out on his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deeply set on' reads as 'determined to', but 'deeply set' is a description of sunken eyes. Anselm Hollo was a Finnish poet and translator who wrote mostly in English.
explanation.definitionFit: Anselm Hollo, born in Helsinki, became a noted experimental poet in America and translated widely from Finnish, German and Swedish.

clue.text: She loved Oliver and Fagin’s position on things?

blocks.note: Fagin, the receiver who trains pickpockets in Oliver Twist, is a con man of sorts
a stance is one's attitude or position on an issue

explanation.surface: The pairing of Oliver and Fagin suggests a question about Dickens's Oliver Twist and the old villain's views.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver and Fagin conjure Oliver Twist, but the Oliver loved here is Oliver Mellors, the gamekeeper in D. H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Constance Chatterley is the aristocratic heroine of Lawrence's novel who falls for her husband's gamekeeper Mellors.

clue.text: “The — welkin cover thou anon With drooping fog as black as Acheron” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream)

definitions.text: “The — welkin cover thou anon With drooping fog as black as Acheron” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream)

blocks.clueFragment: “The — welkin cover thou anon With drooping fog as black as Acheron”
blocks.note: surface reading: an order to blot out the sky with fog as dark as the river of the underworld, with a gap
setter's reading: the source names the Shakespeare comedy whose fairy king speaks the line

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: Oberon tells Puck to cover the night sky with fog so the quarrelling lovers lose each other in the wood. The welkin is an old word for the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: A night sky full of visible stars is the natural adjective for the heavens that Puck must hide behind black fog.

clue.text: Greek character held back by Mark Braddock?

indicators.note: going back means travelling the wrong way, so the letters are read from the end
to be held is to be gripped inside something else, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a grade is a mark given for work
tau is the Greek letter T

explanation.surface: A Greek figure is detained by a man called Mark Braddock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark Braddock' looks like a full name, but Mark is wordplay and Braddock alone is the definition: Benjamin Braddock is the title character of Charles Webb's novel The Graduate.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Braddock, the aimless young man seduced by Mrs Robinson, is known by the novel's title as a recent college leaver.

clue.text: Reconstruction work? We do it when night falls

indicators.note: something that falls collapses into a heap, so the letters tumble into a new order

blocks.note: fifteen letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks about rebuilding work and is told it is done after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reconstruction' looks like building work, but with a capital it is the period after the American Civil War. 'When night falls' sounds like a time of day; 'falls' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Mitchell's novel follows Scarlett O'Hara through the Civil War and the Reconstruction years in Georgia that followed.

clue.text: I make short work of Darling’s fringe in Barrie novel

definitions.note: the setter speaks as the answer, so 'I' is a noun phrase meaning one who shortens works

indicators.note: a fringe runs round the edge, so only the outermost letters are kept
novel means new and different, so the letters take a fresh arrangement
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written
the first and last letters of the name

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of dashing off the Darling children's fringe-cutting episode in a J. M. Barrie novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Darlings are the family in Barrie's Peter Pan, which makes 'Barrie novel' look like a book title; 'novel' is the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An abridger cuts a longer book down to a condensed version, quite literally making a short work of it.

clue.text: Legendary king German theologian doffs cap for?

indicators.note: to doff a cap is to take off what sits on top, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: Martin Luther, the German theologian of the Reformation

explanation.surface: A German theologian raises his hat respectfully to a king of legend.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the cap is the top letter, so beheading the Reformation leader leaves the king.
explanation.definitionFit: Uther Pendragon is the king of Arthurian romance who fathered Arthur with Igraine at Tintagel.

clue.text: Grisham’s novel account sending up vacuous thickie

indicators.note: a vacuous word is empty inside, so only its outer letters are left standing
in a down entry, sending something up lifts it out of its place to move it to the top

blocks.note: a thickie is a stupid person; emptied, the word keeps only its ends
an account, as from a bank or a witness, is a statement

explanation.surface: A Grisham novel tells the story of a stupid character being mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sending up' looks like mockery, but in a down entry it means moving letters to the top: the two letters sit inside the account word already and are lifted out of the middle to lead.
explanation.definitionFit: The Testament is John Grisham's 1999 legal thriller about a billionaire's will leaving everything to an unknown daughter.

clue.text: A network type likely to caution Sopranos writer

blocks.note: taken as written
a LAN is a local area network
someone who issues cautions is a warner

explanation.surface: A TV network person might want to warn the writer of The Sopranos.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sopranos suggests the American TV mob drama, but here it is the 1998 novel about Scottish Catholic schoolgirls in a choir.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Warner is the Scottish novelist of Morvern Callar who wrote The Sopranos, later staged as Our Ladies of Perpetual Succour.

clue.text: Job as a Wells headmaster, or as a reformer

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of Job, the suffering headmaster in H. G. Wells's The Undying Fire
second meaning: the Bohemian church reformer burned at Constance in 1415

explanation.surface: Taking a job as a headmaster in Wells, or as a reformer, sounds like a career choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' looks like employment and Wells like the Somerset cathedral city; in fact Job is a first name and Wells is H. G. Wells, whose The Undying Fire retells the Book of Job through a headmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells named his schoolmaster Job Huss, and Jan Hus, often spelt Huss, was the Czech priest who prefigured the Reformation.

clue.text: Writer Auden ignored for Time Lord role, they say!

indicators.note: whatever is ignored is left out of account, so those letters are dropped
what people say is spoken, so the result is judged by its sound

blocks.note: the Time Lord hero of the long-running BBC science-fiction series
the poet W. H. Auden's initials
with the initials gone, what is left is spoken as doctor-oh

explanation.surface: A writer gets the part of the Doctor once Auden is passed over, people report.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping W and H from the show's title leaves DOCTOR O, which is said the same way as the American novelist's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: E. L. Doctorow was the American novelist of Ragtime, Billy Bathgate and The Book of Daniel.

clue.text: Candleford postmistress and counter staff docked money

indicators.note: counter means running against, so the letters go the opposite way
a docked tail is cut short, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: a rod is a staff or stick
cash is ready money

explanation.surface: A village postmistress and the people behind the counter have had money taken from their pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter staff' reads as shop assistants, but 'counter' is the turnaround signal and staff a stick. Candleford is the town in Flora Thompson's Lark Rise to Candleford.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorcas Lane runs the post office and forge at Candleford Green and takes on young Laura as her assistant in Thompson's trilogy.

clue.text: German novelist who sounds a geezer

indicators.note: how something sounds is about hearing it, so the spelling may differ

blocks.note: geezer is British slang for a man or bloke

explanation.surface: A German novelist is described as talking like a bit of a London lad.
explanation.walkthrough: A geezer is British slang for a man, usually a cheerful working-class one.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Mann was the German author of Buddenbrooks, The Magic Mountain and Death in Venice, and won the Nobel Prize.

clue.text: A way guards tie up a graphic novelist

indicators.note: a guard stands round what it protects, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: taken as written
a lane is a narrow road or way
to moor a boat is to tie it up

explanation.surface: A road with security guards is used to restrain a comic-book author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tie up' sounds like binding a prisoner, but it is what you do to a boat at a quay.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Moore wrote the comic-book novels Watchmen, V for Vendetta and From Hell, landmarks of the form.

clue.text: One tapping mobile veteran holds in hospital

indicators.note: something mobile moves about, so the letters shift into another order
holding something in keeps it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the map and road-sign abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Someone using a mobile phone is an old soldier kept in hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like a phone and 'tapping' like typing on it; in Poe's poem a visitor comes 'tapping, tapping at my chamber door'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's narrator hears a gentle rapping at his door and admits a bird that perches on a bust and croaks Nevermore.

clue.text: A shade tense, having taking on soldiers in wartime work?

indicators.note: taking on extra means picking something up, so one piece is placed ahead of the other

blocks.note: a shade of colour is a tone
soldiers are men, especially other ranks
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Someone a little nervous after taking on troops during the war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shade tense' reads as 'slightly anxious', but a shade is a colour tone and tense is the grammar abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan's novel follows a false accusation in 1935 into the Dunkirk retreat and London hospitals of the Second World War.

clue.text: A tiny thief returned to do over one pulling blade?

indicators.note: returning means going back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to do over is British slang for burgling or robbing a place
a rower pulls an oar, whose flat end is the blade

explanation.surface: A small burglar comes back to ransack a place again, armed with a knife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blade' suggests a knife; it is the end of an oar. To do over a house is British slang for burgling it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Norton's Borrowers are little people living under the floorboards who take, or borrow, what humans leave lying about.

clue.text: Type of elder to put endless value on Hamlet?

indicators.note: with no end, a word stops short and loses its final letter
in an across entry, putting one thing on another means placing it after, so the first-named piece goes second

blocks.note: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, a Dane
worth is value

explanation.surface: A sort of village elder is asked to rate Hamlet as priceless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elder' looks like an old person and Hamlet like a small village; the elder is a shrub and Hamlet is Shakespeare's prince.
explanation.definitionFit: Danewort, or dwarf elder, is a low-growing species of the elder genus Sambucus, said to spring from Danish blood.

clue.text: Slogan alienating foremost American quilt-maker?

indicators.note: to alienate is to drive away, and the foremost is the first in line, so the opening letter is lost

blocks.note: a motto is a slogan or maxim

explanation.surface: A slogan that puts off the leading US quilt manufacturer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quilt-maker' seems to be a craftsperson; it is a novelist, Whitney Otto, whose book How to Make an American Quilt became a film.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitney Otto wrote How to Make an American Quilt, so she is in a sense its maker, hence the question mark.

clue.text: One who launched ships with a lover of Demetrius

blocks.note: Helen of Troy's was the face that launched a thousand ships, in Marlowe's phrase
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman who named ships at launches is seen with a lover of a man called Demetrius.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Launched ships' suggests a dockside naming ceremony; it is Marlowe's line about Helen of Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: In A Midsummer Night's Dream Helena pines for Demetrius, who scorns her until fairy magic turns his heart.

clue.text: “Like to good angels, nothing can —: ’Tis less grief to be foul, than to have been fair” (The Anagram, John Donne)

definitions.text: “Like to good angels, nothing can —: ’Tis less grief to be foul, than to have been fair” (The Anagram, John Donne)

blocks.clueFragment: “Like to good angels, nothing can —: ’Tis less grief to be foul, than to have been fair”
blocks.note: surface reading: lines claiming a plain face, like an angel, cannot be spoiled, with a gap
setter's reading: the source names Donne's elegy, despite its title not a crossword anagram

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue from Donne's mock-praise elegy about an ugly woman: since she is already foul, nothing can make her worse. 'The Anagram' is the poem's title, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To damage or weaken something fits the joke that time and age cannot spoil a face that was never beautiful.

clue.text: Lopsided, like some gardens Woolf cultivated?

blocks.note: as means like
Kew Gardens are the Royal Botanic Gardens in west London

explanation.surface: Virginia Woolf's garden beds were laid out crookedly.
explanation.walkthrough: Kew Gardens is the botanic garden in London and also the title of a Virginia Woolf short story, which she cultivated in the sense of writing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something askew sits crooked or off-centre, the same as being lopsided.

clue.text: One very tight nurse caught in gusty breeze

indicators.note: a gusty wind blows things about, so the letters are scattered into a new order
something caught in something else is trapped inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
EN is an enrolled nurse

explanation.surface: A tightly bandaged nurse gets caught out in a strong wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very tight' suggests something firmly fastened or drunk; it means stingy, as Dickens's Scrooge is.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebenezer Scrooge of A Christmas Carol is the byword for a miser, tight being slang for mean with money.

clue.text: Popcorn writer found in hotel to nibble

indicators.note: what is found in something lies inside it, so the letters sit within the words that follow

blocks.note: the run of letters spans the ending of the first word, the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone writing about popcorn is discovered snacking in a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: Popcorn sounds like the snack, which fits nibbling; it is a 1996 novel about a Hollywood director.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Elton, the British comedian and novelist, wrote Popcorn, a satire on screen violence that won a Gold Dagger.

clue.text: Jester avoiding outskirts of Icelandic city

indicators.note: outskirts are the edges of a town, so only the outer letters count
avoiding something means keeping clear of it, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: Yorick is the dead king's jester whose skull Hamlet holds
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A court fool keeps clear of the suburbs of a city in Iceland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Icelandic city' looks like Reykjavik; the definition is just 'city', and Icelandic only supplies the letters to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: York is the walled cathedral city in the north of England, a word used plainly for city here.

clue.text: Book something seen in a cosmetic dentist’s brochure?

definitions.text: something seen in a cosmetic dentist’s brochure?

blocks.note: first meaning: Zadie Smith's debut novel of 2000

blocks.clueFragment: something seen in a cosmetic dentist’s brochure?
blocks.note: second meaning: the gleaming smile shown off in advertising for whitening treatments

explanation.surface: Booking an appointment after seeing a cosmetic dentist's advertising leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' reads as a verb, to make an appointment, but it is a noun naming a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Zadie Smith's acclaimed first novel follows two families in north London, and dazzling smiles are what cosmetic dentistry sells.

clue.text: Neologism describing Liberal America?

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: a neologism is a newly coined word
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A new political term is coined for left-leaning America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' looks like characterising in words; it is the geometry sense of drawing round. Liberal America sounds like a political label.
explanation.definitionFit: The Americas were called the New World by Europeans after Columbus, as against the Old World of Europe, Asia and Africa.

clue.text: Unknown soldier working at front for a general

indicators.note: being at the front means leading the line, so these pieces are placed ahead

blocks.note: a soldier ant is a worker caste of ant
on means working or operating, as a switched-on machine
y is one of the algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: The Unknown Soldier is serving on the front line on a general's orders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unknown soldier' is a set phrase for the tomb, but the two words split: Unknown is the letter from algebra and soldier the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony was Caesar's general and later Cleopatra's lover, defeated at Actium by Octavian.
